data.rationale: zpl_vec4_mag2 calls zpl_vec4_dot(v,v) and needs to prove \result >= 0.0f. The dot product of a vector with itself equals the sum of squares (v.x*v.x + v.y*v.y + v.z*v.z + v.w*v.w), which is always non-negative. Without this postcondition from zpl_vec4_dot, zpl_vec4_mag2 cannot publish its own non-negativity guarantee to callers.

zpl_vec4_norm calls zpl_vec4_dot(v,v) and passes the result to zpl_rsqrt which requires x > 0.0f. To prove this call-site precondition, we need to know that the returned value equals the float sum of squares, so that our precondition `\add_float(...) > 0.0f` propagates to the result. Without this postcondition the connection between the caller's precondition and the returned value is opaque.

data.message: Published postcondition: ensures \result == \add_float(\add_float(\add_float(\mul_float(v0.x, v1.x), \mul_float(v0.y, v1.y)), \mul_float(v0.z, v1.z)), \mul_float(v0.w, v1.w)); — this gives zpl_vec4_norm the exact float-value identity needed to prove the call-site precondition for zpl_rsqrt.

`ensures \result >= 0.0f` is not provable for arbitrary v0, v1 — the dot product of two different vectors can be negative. It is only non-negative for self-dot (v0 == v1). 

Instead, use the exact-value postcondition now published (demand_2 / v2): `ensures \result == \add_float(\add_float(\add_float(\mul_float(v0.x, v1.x), \mul_float(v0.y, v1.y)), \mul_float(v0.z, v1.z)), \mul_float(v0.w, v1.w));`

When zpl_vec4_mag2 calls zpl_vec4_dot(v, v), substituting v0 == v1 == v gives \result == x*x + y*y + z*z + w*w (sum of squares), which WP should be able to prove is >= 0.0f since each squared float term is non-negative.
